title: Thermal Stratification Drives Hypolimnetic Hypoxia in Low‐Gradient Rivers: Flow Velocity Thresholds for Prevention and Management
content:
ABSTRACT

Hypoxia in marine and lake environments is often linked to thermal stratification; however, in rivers, where turbulence is commonly assumed sufficient to maintain mixing, our understanding of these processes is comparatively limited. The Darling-Baaka River, a lowland river in semi-arid south-eastern Australia, recently experienced hypoxic events that caused mass fish mortalities following rapid mixing after a period of prolonged thermal stratification during low flows. We investigated how depth-averaged flow velocities influence thermal stratification and hypolimnetic hypoxia in three weir pools on the Darling-Baaka River to determine discharge rates required to prevent these events. Discharge was related to flow velocity within each site and stratification was characterised by measuring temperature and dissolved oxygen in surface and bottom waters over 6 months. Persistent thermal stratification affected the two deeper sites, Tilpa and Wilcannia, and hypolimnetic hypoxia (dissolved oxygen saturation < 50%) was common (64.9% and 46.7% of observations), with oxygen depleting to 0%–20% within 5 days of persistent stratification. The shallower site, Pooncarie, did not persistently stratify due to higher flow velocities at similar discharges and hypolimnetic hypoxia occurred in less than 0.1% of observations. Flow velocities greater than 0.06 m s−1 suppressed persistent thermal stratification and supported daily hypolimnetic reaeration. Increasing velocities strengthened mixing and velocities of 0.20 m s−1 almost completely suppressed diel stratification. We suggest that velocities of at least 0.07 m s−1 can suppress persistent thermal stratification and reduce the incidence of associated hypoxic events. Deriving discharge targets from velocity thresholds provides a transferable management framework for comparable environments.
